rules.statement: Recognise revenue to depict the transfer of promised goods or services to customers at the amount of consideration the entity expects to be entitled to.
Apply the five-step model: identify the contract, identify performance obligations, determine the transaction price, allocate it, and recognise revenue as each obligation is satisfied.
Account for a contract with a customer only when all five criteria are met, including approval/commitment, identifiable rights and payment terms, commercial substance, and probable collection.
A contract qualifies only if it is probable the entity will collect the consideration to which it will be entitled for the goods or services transferred.
At contract inception, identify as a performance obligation each promise to transfer a distinct good or service or a series of substantially-the-same distinct goods or services.
A good or service is distinct only if the customer can benefit from it on its own or with readily available resources, and it is separately identifiable in the contract.
Recognise revenue when (or as) a performance obligation is satisfied by transferring control of the promised good or service to the customer.

Recognise revenue over time if the customer consumes benefits as the entity performs, the entity creates/enhances a customer-controlled asset, or the asset has no alternative use with an enforceable right to payment.

If an obligation is not satisfied over time, recognise revenue at the point in time control transfers, indicated by present right to payment, legal title, physical possession, risks and rewards, and acceptance.
Determine the transaction price as the amount of consideration the entity expects to be entitled to in exchange for transferring the promised goods or services.
Estimate variable consideration using either the expected value (probability-weighted) or the most likely amount, whichever better predicts the consideration.
Include variable consideration in the transaction price only to the extent it is highly probable a significant reversal of cumulative revenue will not occur.
Adjust the transaction price for the time value of money when the contract contains a significant financing component.
Need not adjust for a financing component if, at inception, the period between transfer and payment is expected to be one year or less.
Allocate the transaction price to each performance obligation on a relative stand-alone selling price basis.
Recognise as an asset the incremental costs of obtaining a contract if the entity expects to recover them.
May expense incremental costs of obtaining a contract when incurred if the amortisation period would be one year or less.
Recognise as an asset the costs to fulfil a contract when they relate directly to a contract, generate or enhance resources, and are expected to be recovered.
Amortise capitalised contract costs on a systematic basis consistent with the transfer of the goods or services to which the asset relates.
A lessee may elect not to recognise a right-of-use asset and lease liability for short-term leases and leases of low-value assets.
For exempted leases, recognise the lease payments as an expense on a straight-line basis over the lease term or another systematic basis.
Make the short-term lease exemption election by class of underlying asset, and the low-value lease exemption election on a lease-by-lease basis.
At the commencement date, a lessee shall recognise a right-of-use asset and a lease liability.
At the commencement date, a lessee shall measure the right-of-use asset at cost.
Right-of-use asset cost comprises the initial lease liability, payments made at/before commencement less incentives, initial direct costs, and estimated dismantling/restoration costs.

Measure the lease liability initially at the present value of the lease payments not yet paid, discounted using the rate implicit in the lease or, if not readily determinable, the incremental borrowing rate.
Lease payments comprise fixed payments less incentives, index/rate-based variable payments, residual value guarantees, purchase option price if reasonably certain, and termination penalties.
After commencement, measure the right-of-use asset using the cost model unless the revaluation model or investment property fair value model applies.
Under the cost model, carry the right-of-use asset at cost less accumulated depreciation and impairment, adjusted for any remeasurement of the lease liability.
Apply the depreciation requirements of IAS 16 to the right-of-use asset.

Depreciate the right-of-use asset to the end of the asset's useful life if ownership transfers or a purchase option is reasonably certain; otherwise to the earlier of useful life end or lease term end.
Subsequently measure the lease liability by increasing it for interest, reducing it for payments made, and remeasuring it for reassessments and modifications.
Calculate interest on the lease liability to produce a constant periodic rate of interest on the remaining balance.
Inventories shall be measured at the lower of cost and net realisable value.
The cost of inventories comprises all costs of purchase, costs of conversion, and other costs incurred in bringing the inventories to their present location and condition.
Costs of purchase comprise the purchase price, import duties and non-recoverable taxes, and transport/handling, less trade discounts, rebates and similar items.
Allocate fixed production overheads to conversion costs based on the normal capacity of the production facilities.
Assign cost using specific identification for items that are not ordinarily interchangeable and for goods produced and segregated for specific projects.
Assign the cost of interchangeable inventories using the first-in, first-out (FIFO) or weighted average cost formula, applied consistently for similar inventories.
The last-in, first-out (LIFO) cost formula is not permitted under IAS 2.
Write inventories down to net realisable value when their cost may not be recoverable due to damage, obsolescence, or a decline in selling prices.
Reverse a prior inventory write-down, limited to the original write-down amount, when the circumstances that caused it no longer exist or net realisable value increases.
Recognise the cost of an item of PP&E as an asset only if future economic benefits are probable and the cost can be measured reliably.
Measure an item of PP&E that qualifies for recognition at its cost.
PP&E cost comprises the purchase price (net of discounts), directly attributable costs of bringing it to working condition, and the initial estimate of dismantling and restoration costs.
Under the cost model, carry an item of PP&E at cost less accumulated depreciation and accumulated impairment losses.
Under the revaluation model, carry an item of PP&E at a revalued amount equal to fair value at revaluation date less subsequent accumulated depreciation and impairment.
Depreciate separately each part of an item of PP&E whose cost is significant in relation to the total cost of the item.
Recognise the depreciation charge for each period in profit or loss unless it is included in the carrying amount of another asset.
Allocate the depreciable amount of an asset on a systematic basis over its useful life.
Review the residual value and the useful life of an asset at least at each financial year-end.
The depreciation method used shall reflect the pattern in which the asset's future economic benefits are expected to be consumed.
Recognise an intangible asset only if probable future economic benefits will flow to the entity and the cost can be measured reliably.
Measure an intangible asset initially at cost.
Internally generated goodwill shall not be recognised as an asset.
Recognise expenditure on research (or the research phase of an internal project) as an expense when incurred; no intangible asset arises from research.

Capitalise development expenditure only when all six criteria are met: technical feasibility, intention to complete, ability to use/sell, probable benefits, adequate resources, and reliable cost measurement.
Internally generated brands, mastheads, publishing titles, customer lists and similar items shall not be recognised as intangible assets.
Amortise an intangible asset with a finite useful life on a systematic basis over that useful life, reflecting the pattern of benefit consumption.
Do not amortise an intangible asset with an indefinite useful life; test it for impairment instead.
Assess at the end of each reporting period whether there is any indication that an asset may be impaired.
Test goodwill and indefinite-life intangible assets for impairment annually, irrespective of whether any indication of impairment exists.
Recoverable amount is the higher of an asset's (or CGU's) fair value less costs of disposal and its value in use.
Reduce the carrying amount of an asset to its recoverable amount when, and only when, the recoverable amount is less than the carrying amount; the reduction is an impairment loss.
Recognise an impairment loss immediately in profit or loss, unless the asset is carried at a revalued amount in which case it is treated as a revaluation decrease.
If recoverable amount cannot be determined for an individual asset, determine it for the cash-generating unit to which the asset belongs.
Assess at each reporting date whether an impairment loss recognised in prior periods (other than for goodwill) may no longer exist or may have decreased.
An impairment loss recognised for goodwill shall not be reversed in a subsequent period.
Recognise a provision only when there is a present obligation from a past event, an outflow of resources is probable, and a reliable estimate can be made.
Measure a provision at the best estimate of the expenditure required to settle the present obligation at the end of the reporting period.
Where the time value of money is material, measure the provision at the present value of the expected settlement expenditures.
Do not recognise a contingent liability.
Do not recognise a contingent asset; recognise the asset only when realisation of income is virtually certain.
Recognise an expected reimbursement only when it is virtually certain it will be received if the obligation is settled, not exceeding the provision amount.
Functional currency is the currency of the primary economic environment in which the entity operates.
Record a foreign currency transaction on initial recognition by applying the spot exchange rate at the transaction date to the foreign currency amount.
At each reporting date, translate foreign currency monetary items using the closing rate.
Translate non-monetary items measured at historical cost in a foreign currency using the exchange rate at the transaction date.
Recognise exchange differences on the settlement or translation of monetary items in profit or loss in the period in which they arise.
Translate a foreign operation into the presentation currency using closing rate for assets/liabilities and transaction-date rates for income/expenses, recognising differences in OCI.
A qualifying asset is one that necessarily takes a substantial period of time to get ready for its intended use or sale.
Capitalise borrowing costs directly attributable to the acquisition, construction or production of a qualifying asset as part of its cost; expense all other borrowing costs when incurred.
For general borrowings, determine capitalisable borrowing costs by applying a capitalisation rate (weighted average of borrowing costs) to expenditures on the asset.
Begin capitalising borrowing costs when expenditures and borrowing costs are incurred and activities to prepare the asset for its intended use or sale are undertaken.
Suspend capitalisation of borrowing costs during extended periods in which active development of the qualifying asset is suspended.
Cease capitalising borrowing costs when substantially all activities necessary to prepare the qualifying asset for its intended use or sale are complete.
Recognise unpaid current tax for the current and prior periods as a liability, and any excess paid as an asset.
Recognise a deferred tax liability for all taxable temporary differences, except those from initial recognition of goodwill or certain initial-recognition exemptions.
Recognise a deferred tax asset for deductible temporary differences to the extent it is probable that taxable profit will be available against which they can be utilised.
Recognise a deferred tax asset for unused tax losses and credits to the extent it is probable that future taxable profit will be available to utilise them.
Measure deferred tax assets and liabilities at the tax rates expected to apply when the asset is realised or the liability is settled, based on enacted or substantively enacted rates.
Do not discount deferred tax assets and liabilities.
Recognise current and deferred tax in profit or loss, except to the extent it relates to items recognised in other comprehensive income or directly in equity.
Recognise tax relating to items recognised in other comprehensive income or directly in equity in OCI or equity respectively, not in profit or loss.
The statement of cash flows shall report cash flows during the period classified by operating, investing and financing activities.
Operating activities are the principal revenue-producing activities and other activities that are not investing or financing.
Investing activities are the acquisition and disposal of long-term assets and other investments not included in cash equivalents.
Financing activities are activities that result in changes in the size and composition of the contributed equity and borrowings of the entity.
Report cash flows from operating activities using either the direct method or the indirect method.
Disclose cash flows from interest and dividends received and paid each separately and classify them consistently from period to period.
A complete set of financial statements comprises a statement of financial position, statement of profit or loss and OCI, statement of changes in equity, statement of cash flows, and notes.
Prepare financial statements on a going concern basis unless management intends to liquidate the entity or cease trading, or has no realistic alternative but to do so.
Prepare financial statements, except for cash flow information, using the accrual basis of accounting.
Present separately each material class of similar items, and items of a dissimilar nature or function unless immaterial.
Do not offset assets and liabilities, or income and expenses, unless required or permitted by an IFRS.
Present a complete set of financial statements (including comparatives) at least annually.
Present comparative information for the preceding period for all amounts reported in the current period's financial statements.
Retain the presentation and classification of items from one period to the next unless a change is justified by a change in operations or required by an IFRS.
Present current and non-current assets and liabilities as separate classifications in the statement of financial position, unless a liquidity-based presentation is more reliable and relevant.
Classify income and expenses into the operating, investing, financing, income taxes and discontinued operations categories in the statement of profit or loss.
Present an operating profit or loss subtotal in the statement of profit or loss.
Present a profit or loss before financing and income taxes subtotal, unless the entity's specified main business activities make it not meaningful.
Present operating expenses by nature, by function, or a mix, whichever provides the most useful structured summary of the entity's expenses.
Disclose management-defined performance measures (MPMs) with a clear label and a reconciliation to the most directly comparable IFRS-defined subtotal.
